title: Production load replay: batching behavior & tail fairness
content:
Summary:

This note captures results from a focused set of experiments where we replayed slices of production traffic through the continuous-batching scheduler to evaluate batch-size dynamics, timeout interactions, and fairness toward long-running KV-cache requests. The goal: reproduce tail latency regressions observed on 2026-02-28 during a regional spike and explore mitigations that do not degrade aggregated throughput or average latency.

Why replay rather than synthetic load?
- Production arrivals are bursty and correlated with user sessions; synthetic Poisson or uniform traces mask coalescence effects and starvation patterns.
- Replay lets us preserve request length distributions, seq-len correlations, and KV-cache hit/miss skew, which are critical to scheduler behavior.

High-level objectives:
- Reproduce the 99.9/99.99p tail patterns seen in prod.
- Measure how different timeout policies and batch size caps affect both tail and cohort fairness.
- Identify guardrails (soft quota, demotion thresholds, prefill heuristics) that reliably reduce regression risk.

Replay harness and environment:
- Harness: replay-tool v0.9.2 (internal) — consumes gzipped request traces, preserves original timestamps (accelerated by factor), and marks requests with original metadata (user-id hash, token-budget, kv-cache-hit).
- Cluster: 4x p4d.24xlarge (test fleet) scaled to the same model instance image as prod (server v2.3.1 + runtime v1.18).
- Isolation: dedicated namespace, KV cache warmed per-run to configured hit-rate where applicable.
- Observability: per-request microtraces (queue_enter, batch_form, kernel_start, kernel_end, resp_sent), aggregator for quantiles and cohort splits.

Workload slices used:
- slice-A: 30m slice centered on the spike (high concurrency, many short requests)
- slice-B: 1h normal traffic baseline (mixed request lengths, moderate kv-cache hit ~38%)
- slice-C: 15m long-seq heavy (large generation requests, low kv-cache hit)

Metrics captured:
- Latency quantiles: p50/p90/p95/p99/p99.9/p99.99 for end-to-end and queue-to-kernel-start
- Batch size distribution (avg, p90, p99)
- Timeout-induced flush rates (explicit flush vs capacity-triggered)
- Request demotion counts (number of times a request was moved to lower priority queue)
- KV-cache interaction: cache hit/miss breakdown and per-cohort latency
- Throughput (tokens/s) and GPU occupancy

Experiment matrix (high level):
- Baseline (Exp 0): scheduler config identical to prod on 2026-02-28 (for reproducibility)
- Exp 1: Aggressive max-batch cap reduction (cap = 0.6 * baseline) + same timeout
- Exp 2: Timeout increase (tail-safe: timeout *= 1.5) with baseline cap
- Exp 3: Dynamic per-cohort timeout (short for small requests, long for long requests) + baseline cap
- Exp 4: Soft-queue demotion enabled (requests exceeding age threshold demoted) + baseline cap
- Exp 5: Prefill enabled (speculative prefill for likely-followup tokens) + baseline cap

Important notes about config keys used in trials: (these are the internal flags we toggled)
- scheduler.max_batch_tokens
- scheduler.dynamic_timeout_multiplier
- scheduler.per_cohort_timeouts
- scheduler.demote_age_ms
- scheduler.prefill_enabled
- scheduler.softquota_high_water

Key findings (summary):
- Baseline replay reproduced the p99.99 spike reliably on slice-A (same microtrace patterns: long queue waits followed by large coalesced batches that pushed kernel queue at the same time).
- Reducing max_batch_tokens (Exp 1) reduced p99 and p99.9 by ~18–24% on slice-A but increased average token throughput overhead by ~6% (fewer batching efficiency). p99.99 improvement modest (~10%).
- Increasing timeouts globally (Exp 2) smoothed out some tail events but caused larger batches to form, increasing kernel contention and raising p50/p90 slightly — tradeoff not favorable for mixed workloads.
- Per-cohort timeouts (Exp 3) delivered the best balance: short requests benefited from tighter timeouts while long requests were allowed longer waiting windows; p99.9 improved ~25% and throughput drop was <2%.
- Soft-queue demotion (Exp 4) helped slightly for kv-cache-miss-heavy cohorts (reduced their p99 by ~12%) but increased end-to-end latency for demoted requests; fairness improved when demotion threshold tuned conservatively.
- Prefill (Exp 5) reduced downstream kernel latency variance for follow-on requests but had negligible impact on initial request tails; combined with per-cohort timeouts it reduced p99.99 the most in long-seq workloads.

Per-experiment observations and specific traces:
- Exp 0 (baseline): microtraces show groups of small requests queued for >120ms before flush, then large combined batch caused kernel-start backlog of 45–70ms. The backlog maps to long kernel queue length coinciding with sudden tokens/s spikes.
- Exp 1 (cap reduced): batch size p99 dropped from 512 tokens to ~320 tokens; kernel backlog reduced on average but we observed more frequent small-batch kernel invocations (cost impact). Some sequences that previously used KV cache warm prefill missed due to smaller coalesced prefixes.
- Exp 2 (timeout up): long tail events converted into longer queuing with even larger coalesced batches; tail of kernel queue time increased. For slice-C (long-seq) this marginally improved end-to-end but worsened mixed workloads.
- Exp 3 (per-cohort): implemented simple classifier: requests <64 tokens use timeout 12ms; 64–512 use 25ms; >512 use 80ms. This cut starvation for short requests and avoided excessively large coalesced batches. Observed that explicit cohorting needs reliable token-length estimate at admission; admissions that misclassified (approx 2%) produced occasional mismatches but were rare.
- Exp 4 (demotion): demotion age tuned to 110ms reduced p99 for kv-miss cohort but moved some requests to lower-priority queues where kernel throughput was lower; good for protecting latency-sensitive short requests.
- Exp 5 (prefill): for follow-up tokens after prefix responses, speculative prefill lowered time from kernel_end to next kernel_start by ~20ms on hits; policy must be careful not to prefill when cost outweighs probability.

Detailed tradeoffs and cost notes:
- Reducing max batch increases kernel invocation frequency -> potential cost per token rises. Need to quantify run-rate cost delta across committed fleet.
- Per-cohort timeouts require accurate admission metadata (token-length, is-streaming, kv-hint). Adding estimation logic at the API layer is cheap but can mispredict; fallback is to use conservative cohorts.
- Demotion improves fairness but complicates SLO accounting; demoted requests show up in a separate service-class with its own tail behaviors and observability needs.

Immediate recommended mitigations (short term):
- Roll out per-cohort timeout strategy to canary region (apply only to hosted-burst lanes) with conservative thresholds (as in Exp 3).
- Enable soft demotion only for kv-cache-miss cohort with demote_age_ms = 110ms and monitor p99/p99.9 for both primary and demoted lanes.
- Disable global increase of timeout (Exp 2) — avoid until further cost modelling done.

Longer-term work (backlog):
- Implement adaptive cohort classifier using arrival features (headers, size-estimate) to reduce misclassification from 2% -> <0.5% (ENGINF-2564).
- Integrate scheduler telemetry into billing plane to measure cost delta from batching changes across running fleet.
- Simulate hybrid policies (cap + per-cohort + prefill) under varied load shapes to tune softquota thresholds.

Commands / reproducibility notes:
- Replay runs used: replay-tool --trace slice-A.gz --time-accelerate 10x --replay-seed 2026-03-02 --cfg experiments/exp3.toml --outdir /tmp/replay/exp3
- Config snapshots stored in repo PR above. Use trace-subset scripts to build focused slices: tools/trace-subset.py --start 2026-02-28T12:14 --duration 00:30:00 slice-A.gz
- Microtraces exported to /metrics/replay/exp3/*.ndjson; use tools/trace-plot.py for waterfall plots.

Open questions / unresolved risks:
- How representative are the selected slices for global fleet behavior? Need to sample at least 12 different spike windows across regions.
- Cost model: what is the dollar-per-token increase when moving to per-cohort timeouts at scale? We have estimates but need real deployment telemetry.
- Interaction with autoscaler: smaller batches increase GPU invocation frequency and may alter scaling heuristics; need to run scale-sensitive sims.

Next steps (owners & timeline):
- [This week] Canarize Exp 3 (per-cohort timeouts) in us-west-2 on hosted lanes only. Owner: Ethan Park. ETA: 2026-03-13.
- [2 weeks] Add telemetry hooks for demotion lane and cost counters. Owner: Lina Chen. ETA: 2026-03-24.
- [3 weeks] Run region sweep of 12 spike windows and collate results. Owner: Sofia Ramirez. ETA: 2026-04-01.

Notes to self / rough thoughts:
- Consider combining prefill heuristics with a low-cost lightweight predictor for follow-up probability (cheap classifier at API).
- Watch for interaction with KV cache eviction patterns when batch caps shrink — more small batches may cause different cache-access ordering.

References and links:
- Repro trace samples: gs://replay-traces/2026/02/28/spike-12.gz
- Related tickets: ENGINF-2491 (prod spike postmortem), ENGINF-2564 (cohort classifier backlog)
- PR with config: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/842

Appendix: quick table of numeric deltas (slice-A):
- Baseline p99.9: 210ms; Exp1 p99.9: 172ms; Exp3 p99.9: 158ms; Exp5+Exp3 p99.99: down from 490ms -> 360ms
- Throughput (tokens/s) baseline: 25k; Exp1: 23.5k; Exp3: 24.5k

If we can get buy-in for per-cohort timeouts + conservative demotion, I think we can materially reduce the extreme tails without exposing large cost regressions. This doc will be updated with canary results and cost telemetry as they come in.
